statement: In people dependent on opioids, mostly heroin, in supervised withdrawal (14 randomized trials, 750 people on buprenorphine and 615 on clonidine or lofexidine, in a Cochrane review searched to December 2016), buprenorphine compared with clonidine or lofexidine increased completion of withdrawal treatment, from about 45 to about 72 in 100 in the review's illustration (risk ratio 1.59, 95% CI 1.23 to 2.06; 11 trials, 1,264 people), so that about one more person completed for every four treated with buprenorphine. It also lowered average withdrawal scores (standardized difference -0.43, -0.58 to -0.28; 7 trials, 902 people) and kept people in treatment longer (0.92, 0.57 to 1.27; 4 trials, 558 people), in hospital and outpatient settings alike. The number of people with any side effect did not differ detectably (risk ratio 0.93, 0.70 to 1.26; very low certainty); the kinds differed (dizziness, dry mouth and tiredness with clonidine; headache, constipation and nausea with buprenorphine), and only people on clonidine stopped because of side effects (3 small trials, not statistically clear). Two trials were stopped early for benefit, which can overstate effects, and no included trial is described as involving fentanyl. Certainty: moderate. Status: replicated.
plain: In trials of people coming off opioids, mostly heroin, more people finished the withdrawal treatment with buprenorphine than with clonidine or lofexidine: about 72 in 100 against 45 in 100. Withdrawal was milder on average and people stayed longer. Side effects were about as common, but of different kinds. These trials were done before fentanyl was common.
population: People dependent on opioids, mostly heroin, in supervised inpatient or outpatient withdrawal, in 14 randomized trials pooled in a Cochrane review
outcome: Completion of withdrawal treatment, with withdrawal severity, time in treatment and adverse effects reported alongside
magnitude: Completion RR 1.59 (1.23 to 2.06), 11 trials (12 comparisons), 1264 participants, GRADE moderate; illustrative 453 against 721 per 1000; number needed to treat 4 (2.8 to 6.7); inpatient RR 1.74 (1.05 to 2.89), 539; outpatient RR 1.45 (1.12 to 1.88), 725. Mean overall withdrawal score SMD -0.43 (-0.58 to -0.28), 7 trials, 902, moderate (sensitivity -0.37, -0.58 to -0.16). Peak withdrawal SMD -0.43 (-0.74 to -0.13), 6 trials, 521, very low. Time in treatment SMD 0.92 (0.57 to 1.27), 4 trials, 558, moderate. Any adverse effect RR 0.93 (0.70 to 1.26), 493, very low; stopping for adverse effects RR 0.20 (0.04 to 1.15), 134, low.

risk_of_bias.note: Completion is an objective outcome; the subjective withdrawal scores hold without trials at high risk of performance or detection bias. Two trials stopped early are recorded.

inconsistency.note: Heterogeneity above 60% for completion and for time in treatment, as the review rated; the direction is the same in inpatient and outpatient subgroups.

indirectness.note: Worded for supervised withdrawal, mostly from heroin, in trials before fentanyl.

imprecision.note: 1264 participants; the interval excludes no effect.

publication_bias.note: The review asserts none was detected but describes no method; recorded as unknown.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high; inconsistency -1 gives moderate, matching the review's own rating for completion, overall withdrawal score and time in treatment, which the card follows. The side-effect comparison is rated very low to low by the review and is reported as a qualification, not as a benefit. Status replicated: 11 trials from several countries in the same direction.
